teachingNote:
Orange mushroom, ridges running down the stem, autumn woods. Nearly everything a beginner reaches for here is shared by both species, which is why this set is the first one.

What does not separate them: both run their spore-bearing surface down the stem, so 'decurrent' proves nothing. Both drop a whitish print, so the spore print — the technique that saves you from a destroying angel — is useless here. Both cut solid, and both discolour brownish when handled.

What does separate them: chanterelle has false ridges, blunt and forking and continuous with the cap flesh; the jack-o'-lantern has true gills, thin and sharp-edged and separable. The chanterelle comes up alone or scattered from soil, mycorrhizal with oak and beech; the jack-o'-lantern comes up in dense clusters with fused bases from hardwood. And a fresh chanterelle smells of apricot, which the jack-o'-lantern does not.

The substrate check has a trap in it. Jack-o'-lanterns fruit from buried roots, so a cluster can appear to rise straight out of bare ground. Growth habit is what rescues you: fused at the base means wood, whatever the surface says. That is why the set carries both characters instead of one.

Odor is the weakest of the five and the game should treat it that way — rain takes it out, and an individual with weathering above 0.4 will not give it up at all.
